title: First aid and staying safe
outcome:
Basic first aid & health emergencies.
Relationships & staying-safe task.
objectives: Choose early emergency help for an adult who does not respond.
Explain when the recovery position is used and order its steps.
Use learning from the taught weeks to explain safe relationship choices.
vocabulary: Not responding when someone checks for a response.
Regular breaths, rather than gasping or abnormal breaths.
A side position that helps keep the airway open when a person is unresponsive but breathing normally.
A limit that protects a person's needs, comfort or safety.
A promise shown through steady, caring actions.

model.title: Choose the right help
model.story: An adult stops responding while resting. There has been no fall or injury. Character A checks that it is safe to approach, checks for a response and shouts for help. A calls 999 at once on speakerphone and follows the call handler's instructions. The adult is breathing normally.
model.reasoning: The call is made before waiting to finish a breathing check. The call handler can help with checking breathing. With normal breathing and no suspected injury, the recovery position can help keep the airway open. A stays if safe, monitors breathing and tells the call handler about changes.

cases.title: Normal breathing
cases.story: An adult becomes unresponsive while lying down. There has been no injury. Character A has called 999. The call handler confirms normal breathing and guides the helper.
questions: Which position may help keep the airway open?
Which two conditions in the case support that choice?
What must the helper keep checking while help is coming?
cases.answer: The recovery position may be used because the adult is unresponsive, breathing normally and has no suspected injury. The helper follows the call handler, stays if safe and monitors normal breathing and response. Changes are reported at once.

cases.title: Gasping is a warning
cases.story: An adult does not respond and is only gasping. Character B suggests rolling the adult into the recovery position and waiting. Character A has access to a phone.
questions: Why is waiting in the recovery position unsafe here?
cases.answer: Gasping is not normal breathing. A should call 999 immediately on speakerphone, shout for help and follow instructions for CPR. An unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally needs the CPR pathway, rather than the recovery position.

cases.title: A boundary needs support
cases.story: Adult Character A repeatedly demands Adult Character B's passwords and becomes angry when B refuses. B feels unsafe. Another character suggests meeting A alone to settle it.
questions: Which actions are safety warning signs?
Which next step is safer than meeting alone?
Who can help, and what changes if danger is immediate?
cases.answer: Repeated password demands and anger at a boundary are warning signs. B should avoid the suggested meeting, seek a safe place and tell a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. Immediate danger needs emergency help. B does not have to give up the boundary or manage A's behaviour alone.

hinge.question: An adult does not respond and is only gasping. Which action is safest?
options: A. Call 999 immediately and follow instructions for CPR.
B. Use the recovery position and wait.
C. Wait until a trusted adult has arrived before calling.
hinge.reason: Gasping is abnormal breathing. Call immediately; the call handler can guide CPR. Finding an adult must not delay emergency help.
hinge.parallel_question: An adult is unresponsive but breathing normally, with no suspected injury. The emergency call is underway. Which option may help keep the airway open?
parallel_options: A. The recovery position, following the call handler and monitoring breathing.
B. Leaving the adult alone because normal breathing means no help is needed.
hinge.parallel_reason: Normal breathing does not remove the emergency. The recovery position can help, but the helper must keep monitoring and stay if safe.

Supported: Use the choice bank to select the emergency action for each adult case; give one reason.
Order the six recovery-position cards with the reference card; state when the position may be used.
Complete the closing prompts using sentence starters; point to each learner's own evidence.
Independent: Explain the different actions for normal breathing and gasping in the two adult cases.
Order the recovery-position steps and explain the need to monitor breathing.
Complete the five closing tasks and identify evidence from the taught weeks.
Aspire: Compare two plausible actions in each adult case and justify which must take priority.
Explain how suspected injury changes the recovery-position choice without inventing a treatment.
Evaluate the relationship advice in the closing task and improve it using a clear safety reason.

evidence_rows: Two caring actions that meet a fictional child's needs and one explained commitment.
One identified technique in an invented post or advert and one respectful response.
A distinction between disagreement and a safety warning, plus a safe next step.
Correct emergency pathways, recovery-position conditions and an ordered sequence.
An individual reasoned response, a trusted-adult or safeguarding-lead route, and one next step.
misconceptions: Any breathing means the recovery position is the right choice.
Gasping is abnormal breathing. An unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally needs an immediate emergency call and CPR instructions.
A person must settle a frightening conflict alone or keep it secret.
Safety comes first. The character can seek a safe place and tell a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead; immediate danger needs emergency help.
teaching_points: Check scene safety and response. Call 999 immediately for an adult who is unresponsive; shout for help and use speakerphone.
Follow the call handler. Gasping or abnormal breathing is not normal and needs the CPR pathway.
The recovery position helps keep the airway open when an adult is unresponsive, breathing normally and has no suspected injury; keep monitoring.
A safety worry can be shared with a trusted adult or safeguarding lead. A person need not meet alone or give up a boundary to settle a frightening conflict.

recovery_steps: Place the nearer arm at a right angle to the body, with the elbow bent and palm upwards.
Bring the far hand across and hold the back of it against the nearer cheek.
Bend the far knee so that the foot is flat on the floor.
Keep the hand at the cheek and roll the adult towards the helper onto their side.
Adjust the upper leg so the hip and knee are bent at right angles. Gently tilt the head back and lift the chin to keep the airway open.
Stay if safe, monitor normal breathing and response, and report changes to the call handler.
closing_tasks: Two fictional adults care for a child. Name two actions that meet the child's needs and explain one commitment.
An invented post shows a heavily edited picture and claims that everyone should look the same. Identify one media technique and write a respectful response.
Two fictional adults disagree about a plan and both listen. Compare this with repeated password demands and anger at a boundary. Explain which needs a safety response.
For an unresponsive adult, explain the early call for help. Distinguish normal breathing from gasping and order the recovery-position steps for the appropriate case.
Improve the advice to meet an angry character alone. Give a safer next step, a trusted-adult or safeguarding-lead route and one evidence location from the taught weeks.
